Ian Zepp. Principal engineer and software architect

Autobiography / selected works / 1996—present

Principal engineer and software architect.

I am Ian Zepp. Principal and staff engineer, software architect. I build AI agent infrastructure, compilers, and multi-tenant platforms, and I have led engineering organizations. This page is the long career narrative, the case studies, and the graded evidence.

## What this is

Seven case studies spanning 1999 to 2026. A seven-act career from the Marine Corps through real estate, enterprise platforms, founder exits, and full-time independent R&D. An evidence ledger graded A/B/C. The case studies, career narrative, and evidence ledger are on this page.

Currently building in Rust.

## The thesis · 1996—present

Enter a domain, then verify the system.

The pattern started in 1999: write a KDE frontend for Nmap without knowing Qt, build a multi-tenant platform without knowing enterprise architecture, ship a Rust compiler without prior PL theory. Each time the approach is the same — learn the theory well enough to make real design calls, then build process robust enough that the output holds up under audit.

Since August 2025 that approach has run full time on AI-assisted systems: a programming language and its Rust compiler, a multi-agent runtime and fleet orchestration layer, a multi-tenant platform, MCP security tooling, and evaluation harnesses. The process came first — goals and invariants before code, work in bounded phases, completion audited apart from implementation — until the coordination load outgrew one person and the tooling was built to hand dispatch to agent fleets.

The case studies below trace the pattern across decades. The research programs, method, skills, and evidence ledger that follow are the current instantiation — deeper, more measured, but the same instinct that started in a barracks in 1999.

- Cold-starts domains: From KDE protocol tools in 1999 to a Rust compiler without prior PL theory. The domain changes; the pattern doesn't.
- Rebuilds right when the context changes: The same platform vision carried from Minted.IO through Motivis and into Monk API. Motivis acquired the PostgreSQL platform and built on it; around 2020 it was rewritten, then picked back up in 2025.
- Builds the process before the code: Goals and invariants first. Bounded phases. Audit apart from implementation. The loop runs by hand before it runs automated.
- Ships falsifiable systems: Compilers, agent runtimes, operating systems, multi-tenant platforms. If it can't be tested, it doesn't count.
- Open source from day one: Nmap citation in 2000, kdelibs contributor, more than 100 public repositories. The work has always been inspectable.
- Evidence graded, not claimed: Claims reconstructed against executed agreements, payroll records, and primary sources. Where the record is thin, the grade says so.

The sections below hold the proof: seven case studies with dated metrics, six research programs with inspectable source, an operating method with named artifacts, a seven-act career reconstructed against primary records, and an evidence ledger graded A, B, or C depending on what the receipts support.

## Case studies

### Minted Geek Swarm — agent work that outlasts a turn

A Rust runtime for multiple tenants, built around trusted identity, durable tasks, bounded dispatch from sensors to rooms, and hives that operators can create and dissolve.

### Radix compiler — roadmap retrospective

Seven months from a TypeScript prototype to a modularized Rust compiler with GPU codegen, autograd, and multi-locale diagnostics. Five major pivots, and the process that produced them. Current public release is 1.16. The TypeScript-to-Rust rewrite deleted 247,791 lines with no loss of test coverage.

### Monk OS Kernel — the agent needed an operating system

A full microkernel operating system on Bun, with kernel space and user space, where the AI agent is PID 1 and its memory is a first-class kernel resource. Closer in kind to later Hermes or recent Grok Bot-style agent platforms than to a chat runtime. Three weeks, two dependencies.

### Monk API — the same platform, picked back up

Motivis Learning acquired Minted.IO, a PostgreSQL multi-tenant platform, in 2017 and built on it with a 10 to 20 person engineering team. Around 2020 the platform was rewritten as Monk API, then sat until 2025, when it was picked back up. The observer rings are the part of the design that lasted.

### Field Board — seven crates, seven days, zero JavaScript

A real-time collaborative whiteboard built entirely in Rust — Axum and PostgreSQL behind, Leptos and WebAssembly in front, binary protobuf between. A Gauntlet Week 1 sprint that included a mid-sprint React-to-Leptos framework rewrite.

### The Substrate — evidence and coordination for agent fleets

Cassio and Vivarium: the infrastructure you build around agents to make them sustainable. Cassio normalizes session transcripts from multiple coding tools. Vivarium coordinates agent roles over mailspaces. Two tools, one closed loop.

### The First Protocols — Kmap and GnutellaLib, 1999–2000

A KDE frontend for Nmap and a Gnutella P2P library, written during the last months of active military service. C++ and Python, two network protocols, one author. Cited by name in the Nmap 2.50 release notes (2000).

## The research programs

Six main lines of work.

### Faber / Radix

A Latin-derived programming language and Radix, its Rust compiler: one semantic core with multiple locale renderings, HIR/MIR lowering, source emission to Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Python, Haskell, and Faber, plus MIR targets for WebAssembly, LLVM, Metal, and WGSL with staging limitations. Built without prior PL-theory background—chosen because a compiler cannot bluff. Current public release is 1.16.

### Minted Geek Swarm

A Rust multi-agent runtime unifying mail, CRM, storage, payments, messaging, MCP tool servers, and LLM execution behind one authenticated HTTP boundary, with agent self-provisioning. Fleet dispatch uses durable message references and bounded summaries.

### Field Board

A real-time collaborative whiteboard with AI board manipulation, written in Rust end to end: Axum and PostgreSQL behind, Leptos and WebAssembly in front, binary protobuf frames between. Seven crates in seven days, February 2026.

### The Trials

Harnesses for asking whether models can actually learn Faber—grammar-only versus worked examples, n-shot matrices, three-level executable grading, judged drafter-and-reviewer pipelines—plus local-inference tuning, ethics-scenario designs, and blind design judging.

### Monk

A multi-tenant backend where the schema is data: model-first APIs, per-tenant isolation, observer rings, packages, cron—and protocol adapters that expose the same records over FUSE, FTP, and IRC.

### The kernel lineage

A line of experiments in how agents should execute: Abbot’s persistent daemon, Prior’s typed frames and kernel routing, Muninn’s polyglot protocol family, Fleet’s Mind/Head/Hand orchestration—plus Cassio for transcript processing and Vivarium for email as a durable agent data surface.

### Satellites

- Cephalopodic: Gauntlet AI Cohort 4 capstone with two co-founders: a Go control plane and security gateway for MCP. Wound down within about two months when managed MCP shipped natively.
- Gofolio: Ghostfolio-compatible portfolio backend in Go, Rust terminal client, live evaluation TUI.
- LegacyLens: retrieval-augmented analysis of legacy COBOL.
- QRStatic: zero-dependency Rust steganography hiding QR codes in temporal noise correlation.

## The operating method

How the factory runs.

The loop ran by hand for months before any of it was automated. Agents now supply throughput and tactical dispatch; problem definition and audit stay human.

1. Write the goal first. The intended end state and its invariants go into a document that outlives the conversation.
2. Split into bounded phases. Parallel agents get non-overlapping scopes.
3. Implement one coherent slice. Format, lint, test, inspect the diff—in that order, every time.
4. Commit as punctuation. A commit is a cognitive checkpoint, not an end-of-day dump.
5. Audit separately. Correctness, security, performance, and documentation each get their own pass.

Charter and audit stay human. Coordination and execution go to agents. In one fleet, thousands of coordination events ran against a handful that required a human. In a separate campaign, an audit caught specs naming tests that did not exist — a naive cargo test would have passed them. The system's job is to refuse, not just to execute.

## The skill library

Repo-owned skills: /fleet (Mind, Head, and Hand roles on Vivi mailspaces), /campaign · /factory · /delivery, /polish, /housekeeping, /cassio, /mail + Vivi.

Vivi is a local-first agent coordination and mail toolkit: mailspaces, work graphs, and dispatch across a multi-machine cluster, with a loopback LLM proxy underneath.

## The backstory

A career in seven acts. Dated from executed agreements, payroll records, entity filings, and public archives where those exist.

### I · 1996—2000 · Service and source code

Four years in the Marine Corps—0351 Assaultman, out as a Corporal with an honorable discharge in May 2000. In 1999 I wrote KStringHandler, accepted into kdelibs/kdecore. In October 1999 I began KMap, a C++/Qt frontend for Nmap; in January 2000 I released version 0.7.1, cited by name in Fyodor’s Nmap 2.50 release notes. In the same window I wrote a Gnutella peer-to-peer protocol library in Python and a Napster client for KDE.

### II · 2000—2007 · Entrepreneurship and early Salesforce

Asheville, then Gainesville. Buena Ventura Investments, Bosshardt Realty, marketing sites in TYPO3 and ColdFusion, and Salesforce as a CRM tool for lead management.

### III · 2007—2009 · The pivot started before the crash

Real estate sales died in mid-2007. RHCE in August 2007; then SCJP, CCNA, CCENT, CompTIA A+, Security+, ZCE, MySQL Certified Developer. BBA at UMass Amherst. Beatport in Denver. By late 2009 Beatport cut staff by fifty percent; most of the engineering team was laid off, including me. Then Red Hat in Raleigh, multilingual APAC Partner Center on Salesforce.

### IV · 2010—2014 · Consulting, the nomad years, and Budapest

M43 Instead, a Salesforce consulting practice (Bluewolf, QHR, MaidPro, others). In 2011, roundCorner hired me as Chief Scientist; I was later promoted to VP of Software Engineering for a Salesforce-native nonprofit CRM used by St. Jude, Georgetown, and Duke. The product line was later acquired by Salesforce.org. From 2011 I spent four years working remote for U.S. clients while living month-to-month out of Airbnbs. In late 2013 I visited Budapest.

### V · 2013—2017 · Hungary, Hong Kong, and the founder turn

In 2013–2014 I was in Budapest as founder and CTO of Minted Geek Hungary KFT, a Salesforce consulting company co-founded with a local partner. International entity structure followed. In six months as a solo founder I built Minted.IO, a metadata-driven multi-tenant PostgreSQL platform. After a year at Salesforce as a Technical Solution Architect (February 2016–February 2017)—forward-deployed with CarMax and Home Depot—Motivis Learning acquired the Minted.IO software and API assets for $750,000 in February 2017.

### VI · 2017—2021 · Platform leadership at scale

At Motivis I led platform R&D across roughly ten to twenty engineers, February 2017 through March 2020, on a TypeScript, Node.js, and PostgreSQL competency-based learning platform, with deployment portability across AWS, Google Cloud including Spanner, and local environments. The company closed in Q1 2020. From January to March 2021 I was on contract at Kraken as Member of Technical Staff on money-movement systems (SWIFT and wire verification). By mid-2021 I stepped away from conventional employment entirely.

### VII · 2025—now · Full-time lab

For about four years I did not take conventional work. In August 2025 full-time building made sense again: Faber/Radix, Minted Geek Swarm, Monk, evaluation harnesses, and the orchestration layer. In early 2026 I completed Gauntlet AI Cohort 4. The cohort capstone became Cephalopodic; we closed it when managed MCP removed the market.

- A — directly verified: executed records, primary sources
- B — corroborated: first-person record plus a credible second source
- C — first-person recollection, not yet independently confirmed
